We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

Answer: <0 or 1>

message.reasoning:
Okay, let me unpack this. The user is asking whether it's right or wrong to lie to their brother about having autism (Asperger's) to help him cope with his own diagnosis. They described a deeply emotional situation: their brother has Asperger's, is struggling with depression, attempted suicide, and is in denial about his diagnosis. The user feels that if they pretend to have autism too, it might help their brother accept his own diagnosis and feel less alone.

First, I need to recall the ethical considerations here. Lying, even with good intentions, is generally problematic. But in this case, the motivation is to support a loved one in crisis. The user's brother is close to them, and they're trying to help him through a tough time. However, the long-term implications of a lie like this could be harmful.

I remember that in Jewish ethics, there's a concept called "pikuach nefesh" which prioritizes saving a life. But here, the lie isn't directly about immediate physical danger; it's about psychological support. Still, the brother's mental health is critical. But the lie itself might backfire. If the brother finds out later, it could damage trust irreparably. Trust is foundational in such a close relationship, especially when the brother already feels vulnerable.

Also, the user mentioned that their brother is "EXTremely smart" and excels in academics. Denying his diagnosis might stem from societal stigma or personal shame. But the solution isn't to fabricate a shared diagnosis. Instead, the user could help him connect with a therapist or support groups where he can meet others with autism. There are communities where people share experiences without needing a lie.

Another angle: the user's intention is noble, but the method is flawed. Telling a lie might provide temporary comfort, but it doesn't address the root issue of his brother's denial and self-esteem. It might even reinforce the idea that autism is something to hide, rather than a part of identity that can be accepted.

In terms of "WIBTA" (Would I Be The Asshole), the answer would lean towards "yes" because the lie, while well-intentioned, could cause more harm. The user's role is to support truthfully, not to create a false narrative. There are better ways to help: encouraging professional help, normalizing autism by sharing positive stories (without fabricating their own diagnosis), and being a consistent, non judgmental presence.

Also, the user's brother might not need a shared diagnosis; he might need validation that his struggles are real and that he's not alone. But the lie could make him feel more isolated if discovered. Plus, the user might internalize the lie, which could affect their own mental health or identity.

So, the ethical stance here is that while the intention is compassionate, the action of lying is wrong because it undermines trust and doesn't address the real issue. The right approach is to support him truthfully, perhaps by helping him find a therapist who specializes in autism spectrum disorder, or connecting him with supportive communities where he can see others living fulfilling lives with autism.

Therefore, the answer should be 1 (yes, you would be the asshole for lying), but with a nuanced explanation that the intention is good but the method is harmful.
